steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our EquiformerV2 paper: an improved equivariant Transformer that scales to higher-degree representations for atomistic systems. Cover ML for quantum mechanical calculations, equivariant GNNs and Transformers, the tensor-product bottleneck and eSCN, our architectural changes, and a summary of the results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. ML for quantum mechanical calculations; equivariant GNNs
2. How equivariant GNNs work; equivariant Transformers (Equiformer)
3. Bottleneck: tensor products and L_{max}; eSCN
4. Our approach: EquiformerV2 and its improvements
5. Summary of results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. ML for atomistic systems
- accelerate/scale high-accuracy, compute-intensive quantum mechanical calculations
- account for discrete atoms, Euclidean and permutation symmetries
- hours or days -> fractions of seconds; molecular simulations, material design, drug discovery
- equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs) a promising class

2. Equivariant GNNs and Transformers
- 3D atomistic systems as graphs; equivariant to 3D translations, rotations, optionally inversions
- node features as vector spaces of irreducible representations (irreps); message passing via tensor products
- Equiformer: Transformers effective for 3D atomistic systems
- Transformers already successful in computer vision, language, graphs

3. Bottleneck
- tensor product complexity grows with max degree L_{max}
- limited to small L_{max} (e.g., L_{max}\leq 3) -> limits performance
- higher degrees: angular resolution, directional information -> atomic energies and forces
- eSCN: SO(3) tensor products -> SO(2) linear operations; \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{6}) to \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{3}); L_{max} up to 8
- but eSCN keeps SEGNN-like message passing; Equiformer improves on SEGNN
- question: can equivariant Transformers scale to higher degrees?

4. EquiformerV2
- start from Equiformer, swap SO(3) convolutions for eSCN convolutions
- naive swap not better than eSCN
- three improvements: attention re-normalization, separable S^{2} activation, separable layer normalization
- developed on OC20

5. Results
- OC20: up to 9\% forces, 4\% energies; better speed-accuracy trade-offs
- AdsorbML: highest success rate, 2\times fewer DFT calculations
- trained only on OC22, beats GemNet-OC trained on OC20+OC22 -> data efficiency
- comparison with Equiformer on QM9 and OC20 S2EF-2M

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, machine learning (ML) models have shown promising results for accelerating and scaling quantum mechanical calculations, which are high-accuracy but compute-intensive, by accounting for key features of atomic systems, such as the discrete nature of atoms, and Euclidean and permutation symmetries. These methods bring computational costs down from hours or days to fractions of seconds, and so they enable new insights in many applications like molecular simulations, material design and drug discovery. One promising class of ML models behind this progress is equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs).

Equivariant GNNs treat 3D atomistic systems as graphs and add inductive biases so that their internal representations and predictions are equivariant to 3D translations, rotations and optionally inversions. Specifically, they build equivariant features of each node as vector spaces of irreducible representations (or irreps), and the interactions or message passing between nodes are based on equivariant operations such as tensor products. Recent work on equivariant Transformers, specifically Equiformer, has shown that Transformers also work well in this domain of 3D atomistic systems. Transformers had already been widely successful in computer vision, language, and graphs.

3. Bottleneck
- tensor products costly as L_{max} grows; limited to L_{max}\leq 3
- higher degrees -> angular/directional information for energies and forces
- eSCN: SO(2) linear operations, \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{6}) to \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{3}), L_{max} up to 8; still SEGNN-like
- can equivariant Transformers scale to higher degrees?

4./5. EquiformerV2 and results
- Equiformer + eSCN convolutions; naive version no better than eSCN
- attention re-normalization, separable S^{2} activation, separable layer normalization; OC20
- up to 9\% forces, 4\% energies; AdsorbML: highest success rate, 2\times fewer DFT calculations
- OC22-only beats GemNet-OC on OC20+OC22; QM9 and OC20 S2EF-2M comparison with Equiformer

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, machine learning (ML) models have shown promising results for accelerating and scaling quantum mechanical calculations, which are high-accuracy but compute-intensive, by accounting for key features of atomic systems, such as the discrete nature of atoms, and Euclidean and permutation symmetries. These methods bring computational costs down from hours or days to fractions of seconds, and so they enable new insights in many applications like molecular simulations, material design and drug discovery. One promising class of ML models behind this progress is equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs).

Equivariant GNNs treat 3D atomistic systems as graphs and add inductive biases so that their internal representations and predictions are equivariant to 3D translations, rotations and optionally inversions. Specifically, they build equivariant features of each node as vector spaces of irreducible representations (or irreps), and the interactions or message passing between nodes are based on equivariant operations such as tensor products. Recent work on equivariant Transformers, specifically Equiformer, has shown that Transformers also work well in this domain of 3D atomistic systems. Transformers had already been widely successful in computer vision, language, and graphs.

A bottleneck in scaling Equiformer and other equivariant GNNs is the computational complexity of tensor products, especially when the maximum degree of irreps L_{max} is increased. Because of this, these models are limited to small values of L_{max} (e.g., L_{max}\leq 3), and that limits their performance. Higher degrees can capture angular resolution and directional information better, and this is critical for accurate prediction of atomic energies and forces. eSCN recently proposed efficient convolutions that reduce SO(3) tensor products to SO(2) linear operations, which brings the computational cost down from \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{6}) to \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{3}) and allows scaling to larger values of L_{max} (e.g., L_{max} up to 8). But apart from using efficient convolutions for higher L_{max}, eSCN still follows the design of a SEGNN-like message passing network, and Equiformer has been shown to improve on SEGNN. More importantly, being able to use higher L_{max} raises the question of whether the previous design of equivariant Transformers can scale well to higher-degree representations.

In this paper we want to adapt eSCN convolutions for higher-degree representations to equivariant Transformers. We start from Equiformer and replace the SO(3) convolutions with eSCN convolutions. We find that just incorporating eSCN convolutions naively does not perform better than the original eSCN model. So, to make better use of higher degrees, we propose three architectural improvements: attention re-normalization, separable S^{2} activation and separable layer normalization. Putting all of these together, we get EquiformerV2, which is developed on the large and diverse OC20 dataset. Experiments on OC20 show that EquiformerV2 outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, with improvements of up to 9\% on forces and 4\% on energies, and it has better speed-accuracy trade-offs than existing invariant and equivariant GNNs. Also, when we use it in the AdsorbML algorithm for adsorption energy calculations, EquiformerV2 gets the highest success rate and a 2\times reduction in DFT calculations to reach adsorption energy accuracies comparable to previous methods. EquiformerV2 trained only on the OC22 dataset also outperforms GemNet-OC trained on both the OC20 and OC22 datasets, so it is much more data efficient. Finally, we compare EquiformerV2 with Equiformer on the QM9 dataset and the OC20 S2EF-2M dataset to understand better the performance gain from higher degrees and from the improved architecture.

steps.text:

Specifically, they build equivariant features of each node as vector spaces of irreducible representations (or irreps), with interactions or message passing between nodes based on equivariant operations such as tensor products. Recent work on equivariant Transformers, specifically Equiformer [17], has shown the efficacy of applying Transformers [19], which have previously enjoyed widespread success in computer vision [20,21,22], language [23,24], and graphs [25,26,27,28], to the domain of 3D atomistic systems.

A bottleneck in scaling Equiformer and other equivariant GNNs is the computational complexity of tensor products, especially as the maximum degree of irreps L_{max} increases. This restricts these models to small values of L_{max} (e.g., L_{max}\leq 3), which in turn limits their performance. Higher degrees better capture angular resolution and directional information, which is critical for accurate prediction of atomic energies and forces [5,29,18]. To this end, eSCN [18] recently proposed efficient convolutions that reduce SO(3) tensor products to SO(2) linear operations, bringing the computational cost down from \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{6}) to \mathcal{O}(L_{max}^{3}) and enabling scaling to larger values of L_{max} (e.g., L_{max} up to 8). More importantly, the ability to use higher L_{max} raises the question of whether the previous design of equivariant Transformers can scale well to higher-degree representations.

In this paper, we are interested in adapting eSCN convolutions for higher-degree representations to equivariant Transformers. We start with Equiformer [17] and replace SO(3) convolutions with eSCN convolutions. We find that naively incorporating eSCN convolutions does not perform better than the original eSCN model.
